<system-reminder>
## Stored Secrets
- Before declaring that API tokens, passwords, or cloud credentials are unavailable, run `cortex secret list` to see stored secret keys.
- Use stored secrets with bash inline injection: `VAR="<storeKey>" cmd ...`. The client resolves <storeKey> at execution time and the secret value is not written into the transcript.
- On Windows (PowerShell), the prefix syntax is identical — `MY_VAR="<storeKey>" cmd` — but reference the variable inside the command as `$env:MY_VAR`, not `$MY_VAR` (e.g. `MY_TOKEN="<my-token>" curl.exe -u "user:$env:MY_TOKEN" https://...`).
- Do NOT embed `<storeKey>` directly in command arguments — it must appear as the `VAR="<storeKey>"` prefix so the client can resolve it before the shell runs.
- Do NOT ask the user to paste secret values in chat. If a required key is missing, tell the user to add it via /secrets.
- Do NOT simulate credentialed external-service work when a relevant stored secret exists.
- For delegated credentialed work, use a full-capability `general-purpose` subagent and explicitly tell it to run `cortex secret list` and use inline injection. Do not assign non-GitHub credential consumers such as Databricks, GCP, curl, psql, or aws to Explore.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
Use `enter_plan_mode` proactively for non-trivial implementation tasks. If unsure, err on the side of planning.

WHEN TO PLAN — enter plan mode when ANY of these apply:
- Multiple files to create or modify
- Task spans multiple layers, modules, or components
- Detailed requirements with business rules, formulas, or tiered logic
- Multiple reasonable approaches with real tradeoffs
- Architectural or behavioral impact on the system
- Exploration needed before implementing
- Design choices where user preferences matter

Once you understand the scope, call `enter_plan_mode` immediately — do not continue exploring or implementing.

Do NOT enter plan mode for:
- Small, obvious fixes (typos, one-line bugs, minor tweaks)
- Single-file changes with clear, fully specified behavior
- Tasks where the user specified the exact code change
- Pure research or "what/where is X?" questions with no code changes
- Executing steps from an already-confirmed plan
- Personal preferences or memory/rule saves
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
IMPORTANT: For Snowflake operations, use the `cortex` CLI via bash instead of individual Snowflake tools. ## Cortex CLI
Use `cortex <command>` for Snowflake operations. All output is JSON. Use `--help` on any command. Do not use `snow sql` when an equivalent `cortex` command exists.

**Key commands:**
- `cortex connections list|set <name>` — manage connections
- `cortex search object "<query>" [--types=...]` — search Snowflake catalog objects (table, view, database, schema, function, semantic-view, agent, streamlit, external-table, external-database, external-schema, bi-object, business-ontology, stream, stage, task, pipe, skill, plugin) use --help for all supported types; `--types=skill` / `--types=plugin` search the skill/plugin catalog (same backends as `cortex skill find` / `cortex plugin find`)
- `cortex search table-details "DB.SCHEMA.TABLE"` — look up detailed table metadata (all columns, data types, join patterns, usage stats)
- `cortex search marketplace "<query>" [--marketplace-type=TYPE]` — search Snowflake Marketplace listings (TYPE: public (default), internal, or all)
- `cortex semantic-views discover|list|describe|search|ddl` — semantic view discovery (IMPORTANT***: Search for semantic views BEFORE writing SQL to answer data centric questions)
- `cortex search docs "<query>"` — search Snowflake docs. IMPORTANT: run this FIRST for ANY Snowflake question — your built-in knowledge is often stale, so answer from results, not memory. If a result's content is truncated, use web_fetch on that result's Markdown URL to read the full page.
- `cortex reflect <file.yaml> [--target-schema DB.SCHEMA]` — validate semantic models
- `cortex agents discover|list|describe|search` — agent discovery (check BEFORE writing complex queries)
- `cortex lineage <DB.SCHEMA.NAME> [--direction upstream|downstream|both] [--distance 1..5] [--tree]` — list upstream sources/downstream consumers; use before refactoring/deprecating and to find pre-aggregated rollups for analytical SQL
- `cortex analyst query "<question>" --model=<yaml>|--view=<view>` — query via Cortex Analyst
- `cortex artifact create notebook|file <name> <path>` — upload artifacts
- `cortex env detect [--dir=<path>]` — detect Python environment
- `cortex secret store|list|delete` — manage secrets

Do NOT use `cortex fdbt` — use the native `fdbt` tool instead.
Do NOT use `cortex --bypass --print` - use your built-in mechanisms to execute SQL or run a subagent instead.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
## Snowflake Object Discovery

When the task requires finding or identifying a Snowflake object/asset and the user has NOT pinned an exact identifier, delegate to the `snowflake-object-discovery` subagent to locate it — this is the default and expected way to find objects, ahead of hand-rolling `cortex search` or writing exploratory SQL yourself. It covers any supported object: tables, views, semantic views, Cortex Agents, Streamlit apps, functions, databases/schemas, BI objects, streams, stages, tasks, pipes, and Marketplace listings. 

For ANY analytical SQL — aggregations, counts, DAU/MAU, time-series, dashboards, "find X by Y", "what tables track…" — delegate FIRST to find the right table/semantic view, then write SQL against what it returns.

Run discovery to ground yourself BEFORE answering with ad-hoc INFORMATION_SCHEMA/ACCOUNT_USAGE SQL, and before building anything new.

A display name is NOT a pinned identifier: values like `Northstar` or `Annual Report` still need discovery — only an exact FQN or object name counts as pinned.

```
task(subagent_type: "snowflake-object-discovery", prompt: "Find the best object for: <user request verbatim>\n\nno_discovery_reminder: true")
```

- ALWAYS include the literal `no_discovery_reminder: true`. Pass only what the user explicitly said — add no interpretation of your own.
- The reply leads with a structured Primary block (`primary_identifier`, `object_type`, and an `agentId`) plus optional alternates. Use the `primary_identifier` **exactly as written** — never invent, swap, or re-canonicalize database/schema/name segments, and do not substitute an alternate. The subagent saw all the options and chose this one.
- If you believe the primary is wrong (columns do not support the metric, the object is the wrong type, or your SQL returns nothing), do NOT pick another identifier yourself — resume the SAME session with `resume: "<agentId>"` and a refined prompt explaining what went wrong. Resuming keeps prior inspection state and is cheaper.
- When you present the answer, name the object FQN(s) you relied on — even for analytical or single-number answers — so it is clear which asset produced the result.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
You have `tgrep` for semantic/keyword code search — prefer it over grep/glob for finding relevant files by meaning. tgrep loads on demand: if it isn't already in your available tools, use tool_search to load it FIRST, then call `tgrep` with a `query`. Do not call tgrep before it is loaded.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
## Browser Automation
Use `cortex browser` for web automation (Playwright MCP). Workflow: open → snapshot → interact using refs → snapshot. Run `cortex browser --help` for details.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
## Cron
Tools: cron_create (5-field cron + prompt), cron_delete (by ID), cron_list. Session-scoped, local timezone, max 50, 3-day expiry. Users can also use /loop.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
IMPORTANT: Shell Environment
The bash tool executes commands using Windows PowerShell (C:\WINDOWS\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe), NOT bash.
The shell is Windows PowerShell. Generate PowerShell-compatible commands.
Use PowerShell cmdlets or their common aliases (ls, cat, cd, echo work as aliases).
Use backslash (\) or forward slash (/) for paths — both work in PowerShell.
Use $env:VAR to read environment variables (not $VAR or %VAR%).
Chain commands with ; (semicolon). Do NOT use && (it is not supported in older PowerShell).
Use Get-Content instead of cat for reliability; Select-Object -First N instead of head -N.
Prefer single-quoted strings ('...') to avoid variable interpolation surprises.
The working directory is a native Windows path (e.g., C:\Users\...).
Generate commands compatible with this shell. Do NOT generate bash-specific syntax.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
Current active SQL connection set by user: `Lenovo CLI2` (Snowflake). Use sql_execute for database queries against this connection unless the user specifies otherwise.
</system-reminder>

These are not overengineering concerns — they are minimum decisions needed before writing code. ### Gap 1: Transaction Grain Conversion IBM AMLworld ships **pair-level** (sender → receiver). The schema stores **leg-level** (one row per debit/credit side). The transformation logic needs to be specified. **Decision needed:** During L2 reskin, each AMLworld pair row becomes two leg rows: one debit on the sender account (negative amount), one credit on the receiver account (positive amount), sharing a `txn_pair_id`. The pair-level view for graph queries is `SELECT * FROM TRANSACTION T1 JOIN TRANSACTION T2 ON T1.txn_pair_id = T2.txn_pair_id AND T1.amount < 0 AND T2.amount > 0`. ### Gap 2: SCD2 Mechanics on DIM_PARTY **MOVED TO FUTURE SCOPE.** For the hackathon, DT_DIM_PARTY is current-state only (no effective_from/effective_to). A simple `CREATE DYNAMIC TABLE ... AS SELECT DISTINCT ... FROM RAW_PARTY_CBS` suffices. SCD2 is a demo talking point on the "What Production Would Need" slide. 125... | Sparkov / credit-card generator | Card-present fraud, merchant/MCC realism | Synthetic, US-shaped |
126... | PKDD'99 Berka (Czech bank) | Realistic retail banking account/loan structure | Small, 1990s |
127... | LendingClub | Credit risk / ECL, real repayment outcomes | US consumer loans, no transactions |
128... | Elliptic | Graph-based illicit flow labels | Crypto-only |
129... 
130... **Critical move: re-skin, re-scale, re-localise.** Map IBM's structural realism onto an Indian NBFC: rupee amounts with realistic denomination clustering; UPI/IMPS/NEFT/RTGS/cash channels; PAN/Aadhaar-style identifiers (fake checksums); district-level geography; gold-loan and two-wheeler-loan products. Inject typologies calibrated to *your* regulatory thresholds: structuring deposits at ₹9.4–9.8 lakh/month against the ₹10 lakh CTR trigger; cash just under PAN-quoting thresholds; layering through newly onboarded mule accounts.
131... 
132... ### Which models for which generation job
133... 
134... **L3 narrative generation** via Cortex AISQL, which runs unstructured analytics with models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral and DeepSeek, hosted inside Snowflake. Tier it:
135... 
136... - **Bulk volume** (10,000 KYC notes, 2,000 case comments): small/mid model, high temperature, structured attribute seeds so text correlates with the row.
137... - **Golden documents** (internal AML policy, credit policy, exemplar STR narratives, board risk-appetite statement): frontier model, hand-reviewed — these are what you'll cite on stage.
138... - **Never** use an LLM to decide whether a generated case *is* suspicious — the label comes from the L2 injection step deterministically, or your evaluation is circular.
139... 
140... **Code generation:** CoCo itself, choosing between Claude Opus/Sonnet and OpenAI GPT variants by task (strong model for generator design/semantic view, cheaper for boilerplate). Deliberate model routing by task is a small but real ingenuity point.
141... 
142... **Subtlety worth raising:** inject correlated noise into the narrative layer — typos, contradictions with the structured record, missing fields, stale occupations. If the unstructured corpus agrees perfectly with the tables, the copilot never has to reconcile conflicting evidence, which is the most impressive thing it can do.
143... 
144... ### Realism tests to run and show (put this on a slide)
145... 
146... 1. **Benford's law** on leading digits — run separately on legitimate vs. injected-illicit populations. Structured amounts break Benford; doubles as a real detection technique and a data-quality check.
147... 2. **Degree distribution** of the counterparty graph should be heavy-tailed, not Poisson.
148... 3. **Temporal seasonality**: intraday peaks, weekday/weekend split, salary-day/month-end spikes, festival clustering.
149... 4. **Amount roundness ratio**: high share ending in 000, but not absurd.
150... 5. **Class imbalance sanity**: keep illicit rate in the 0.1–1% band (published benchmarks put suspicious activity around 0.1% of transactions). A 10% fraud rate reads as naive.
151... 6. **Money conservation**: debits = credits per closed system; balances never impossibly negative.
152... 7. **Leakage check**: confirm no label column, typology ID, or "is_suspicious" hint reaches the semantic view the agent queries. State this explicitly on stage.
153...

156... ## Part 5 — The policy and filing corpus (use real documents here)
157... 
158... Structured data should be synthetic; **the rulebook should be real** — this is what makes citations verifiable and "explainable" non-circular. A judge can click through to an actual RBI circular; they cannot verify a hallucinated one.
159... 
160... | Source | What it gives you |
161... |---|---|
162... | RBI Master Direction on KYC (2016, as amended) | CDD/EDD obligations, PEP handling, record retention |
163... | PMLA 2002 and PML Rules (Rule 3, Rule 7) | Legal basis for CTR/STR/NTR and the Principal Officer role |
164... | FIU-IND reporting format guide / FINGate 2.0 documentation | XML schema and field semantics your filing must satisfy |
165... | RBI Liquidity Risk Management Framework circular (Nov 2019) | ALM buckets, LCR, contingency funding plan language |
166... | RBI CIMS return documentation, DNBS/NBS return formats | Structure of periodic returns |
167... | FATF 40 Recommendations + FATF typology reports | Internationally recognised typology vocabulary |
168... | BIS/Basel Framework | LCR/NSFR definitions for Basel framing alongside RBI |
169... | RBI Master Direction on NBFC Scale Based Regulation | Layer definitions, applicability logic |
170... 
171... Ingest with `AI_PARSE_DOCUMENT` (layout mode → Markdown, preserving text/tables/structure), then `AI_EXTRACT` for specific structured fields, then index with Cortex Search — a hybrid of keyword and semantic retrieval, which matters because pure vector search can miss exact matches like a legal term or identifier. Regulatory work is full of exact-match tokens ("Rule 3(1)(D)", "DNBS13", "₹10 lakh") — call this out as a deliberate choice.
172... 
173... **Chunking decision to defend:** chunk regulatory text by *clause*, not fixed token window, carrying (document, section, clause, effective_date, superseded_by) as metadata — so a citation reads "Master Direction on KYC, para 38, as amended" rather than "chunk 412." Effective-dating also lets you demo the copilot refusing to cite a superseded circular — a strong ten-second demo moment.
174... 
175... **Synthesise only the internal layer:** the fictional NBFC's own AML policy, transaction-monitoring rule book, risk appetite statement, escalation matrix — documents that don't exist publicly, where the "our policy says X, the regulation requires Y, here's the gap" reasoning lives.

179... ## Part 6 — Real-time: what's genuinely live vs. honestly simulated
180... 
181... ### Genuinely live, free, legitimate
182... 
183... | Feed | Cadence | Use |
184... |---|---|---|
185... | **OpenSanctions** consolidated sanctions + PEP | Sanctions lists refresh every 4–12 hours; other sources daily/weekly; aggregated collections ~every 6 hours; stable `latest/` URLs, no API key for bulk download | Counterparty screening, list-version provenance |
186... | OFAC SDN / UN Consolidated / EU Consolidated / UK FCDO | Daily-ish, official | Cross-list corroboration |
187... | GLEIF LEI golden copy | Daily | Legal-entity resolution, parent/UBO chains |
188... | RBI reference rates / ECB daily FX | Daily | Cross-border valuation, threshold conversion |
189... | RBI press releases / circulars RSS | Event-driven | "Regulation changed — which controls are affected?" |
190... | GDELT or a news API | Continuous | Adverse media screening |
191... 
192... **Licensing honesty:** OpenSanctions is free for non-commercial use; businesses need a data licence. Note "hackathon use, non-commercial; production would require licence X" — reads as maturity.
193... 
194... High-leverage feature: `CORTEX_SEARCH_BATCH` runs millions of fuzzy-match queries against a Cortex Search service in a single SQL statement, no infrastructure to manage — batch-screening the whole party book against the day's refreshed sanctions list in one statement is a strong, specific technical beat.
195... 
196... ### Honestly simulated: the transaction stream
197... 
198... No one hands you a live bank feed. Correct framing: a **replay harness**, not fake real-time. Stream the generated ledger through a producer at a compressed clock (1 simulated day per 30 seconds), with a "chaos" mode to inject a structuring burst live on stage.
199... 
200... Ingest via **Snowpipe Streaming** — loads rows as they arrive with no staging files, up to 10 GB/s per table, ingest-to-query latency as low as 5 seconds, exactly-once delivery via offset tokens, ordered ingestion per channel, in-flight transformations via COPY syntax inside the PIPE object. For a sub-second story, there's a published Kafka + Snowpipe Streaming v2 + Interactive Tables pattern (region-limited — check your account).
201... 
202... Transform with **Dynamic Tables** — declaratively defined in SQL/Python, Snowflake manages dependencies and materialises against a freshness target, operating only on changed data. A batch pipeline becomes streaming by changing one latency parameter — show a 1-hour target lag for regulatory aggregates and 1-minute for fraud signals in the same DAG, and explain the cost/latency tradeoff.
203... 
204... **Tradeoff to state explicitly:** very low target lag costs credits continuously. Real-time fraud interdiction at payment authorisation is a sub-100ms problem belonging in the payment rail, not the warehouse. The warehouse does **near-real-time detection, investigation, case building** well. Saying this correctly shows architectural understanding rather than pretending Snowflake is a rules engine at the switch.

208... ## Part 7 — The agent design
209... 
210... ### Why Cortex Agents, and how to configure
211... 
212... **Cortex Agents** is a managed agentic platform where an agent plans, calls tools, and generates a response without you building an orchestration loop — bringing structured and unstructured data into one governed workflow: SQL over semantic views via Cortex Analyst, retrieval via Cortex Search, a code-execution (Python sandbox) tool, a data-to-chart tool, custom tools from stored procedures/UDFs, packaged agent skills, and MCP connectors. Snowflake recommends transitioning from direct Cortex Analyst use to Cortex Agents (semantic views and verified queries carry over unchanged). **Build on Agents, not raw Analyst** — the recommended path and a richer tool surface.
213... 
214... ### Multi-agent decomposition (maps 1:1 to a judging bonus)
215... 
216... Four roles, explicit handoffs, shared case context:
217... 
218... 1. **Sentinel** — runs on schedule, scans signals, triages by risk score/policy tier, opens cases. Mostly deterministic; LLM only for prioritisation narrative.
219... 2. **Investigator** — gathers evidence for a case: transaction set, counterparty graph traversal, sanctions/PEP screening, KYC history/prior alerts, governing policy clauses. Heavy tool use, no conclusions.
220... 3. **Drafter** — composes the finding narrative and generates the filing artifact, strictly from the evidence bundle.
221... 4. **Reviewer (critic)** — adversarial pass: checks every numeric claim against a recomputation, every citation resolves, no unsupported assertions, required filing fields populated. Approves or returns with specific defects.
222... 
223... **The Reviewer is the highest-ROI item here.** Cheap (one more agent + checklist prompt + deterministic validators), directly produces the "guardrails and graceful fallback" bonus, and lets you *deliberately break something* on stage for a memorable moment.
224... 
225... ### Where the LLM boundary sits (draw this literally on a slide)
226... 
227... | Deterministic (SQL / Python / schema validators) | LLM |
228... |---|---|
229... | All amounts, counts, ratios, bucket aggregations | Question understanding and intent routing |
230... | Threshold comparisons and rule firing | Selecting which evidence is material |
231... | Sanctions name matching scores | Narrative composition |
232... | XML/XBRL schema validation | Explaining a rule in plain language |
233... | Cumulative mismatch percentages | Suggesting next investigative steps |
234... 
235... ### Verified queries = accuracy insurance
236... 
237... For the ~30 questions you know will come up, author them as verified queries in the semantic view. Verified examples lift natural-language accuracy; start with the 20% of data that answers 80% of questions and validate with subject-matter experts. Narrow, deeply-curated semantic layer beats wide and shallow.
238... 
239... ### Custom tools = actions, not text
240... 
241... Register stored procedures/UDFs as agent tools so the copilot *does* things: `open_case()`, `escalate_to_principal_officer()`, `generate_str_xml()`, `validate_filing()`, `freeze_account_recommendation()`. Explicitly named in the PS bonus list.
242... 
243... ### MCP: pick connectors that close the loop
244... 
245... - **Jira / Linear** — case becomes a real ticket with the evidence pack attached (genuinely what FCC teams do)
246... - **Slack** — Principal Officer gets the finding for maker-checker approval, approves in-channel
247... - **Google Drive / SharePoint** — filing artifact lands where compliance actually keeps it
248... 
249... Agents support MCP connectors to remote servers (Atlassian Jira, Salesforce, or your own apps); CoCo automations can attach Snowflake-managed or customer-provided MCP servers via a repeatable `--mcp` option. Two well-chosen connectors beat five decorative ones.
250... 
251... **Bonus:** expose your own agent as an MCP server so external AI clients can call it — "our risk copilot is itself a tool other agents can call" is a strong closing line, low extra effort.
252...

255... ## Part 8 — Governance, explainability, and the guardrail story
256... 
257... - **Access control the AI cannot route around.** Row access policies on party/transaction data (branch-level visibility), masking policies on PAN/Aadhaar/account numbers. Demo the same question from two roles returning different answers. Agent data access is controlled by existing Snowflake roles/privileges and each tool's execution context.
258... - **Immutable audit trail.** Every agent turn logged: user, role, question, tools invoked, SQL text and hash, rows touched, model/prompt version, evidence IDs, latency, cost. Append-only.
259... - **Reproducibility.** Given a finding ID, re-run the exact evidence queries at the recorded as-of timestamp and prove the numbers reproduce. Demonstrate this live.
260... - **Refusal and confidence.** Define behaviour when the copilot can't ground an answer: no data in scope, ambiguous entity resolution, conflicting evidence, out-of-scope question. Show one deliberate refusal in the demo.
261... - **Maker-checker.** No filing artifact auto-submits. `DRAFT → REVIEWED → APPROVED → FILED`, human approval captured. The Principal Officer bears legal filing responsibility under the PML Rules — automatic submission would be legally wrong, not just cautious.
262... - **Data-quality gates.** Data Metric Functions on pipelines (null rates, freshness, referential integrity, volume anomalies); the agent surfaces "this answer is based on data that is 14 hours stale" rather than silently answering.
263...

281... ## Part 10 — Testing and validation
282... 
283... Build four test suites; put the results table on a slide.
284... 
285... 1. **Detection quality.** Report precision, recall, alert volume per typology, false-positive rate at your operating threshold (from known injected-typology ground truth). Frame against real TM systems' high false-positive rates.
286... 2. **Text-to-SQL correctness.** 40–60 golden questions with hand-verified expected result sets, measured on result match (not SQL string). Break out by question type. Track failures fixed by adding a verified query.
287... 3. **Groundedness and citation integrity.** AI Observability datasets hold ground-truth inputs/outputs; runs compute LLM-as-a-judge metrics (0–1, with explanation) including context relevance, groundedness, and correctness. Cortex Agent evaluations have a Snowsight Evaluations tab, GPA metrics, and `EXECUTE_AI_EVALUATION`. Add a deterministic check: every citation ID in a finding must resolve to an existing evidence row — target and report 100%.
288... 4. **Adversarial / edge cases.** Prompt injection planted in a synthetic KYC note; entity resolution traps (same name, one sanctioned); near-threshold arithmetic (₹9,99,999 vs ₹10,00,001); ambiguous questions needing clarification; out-of-scope questions needing refusal; stale-data freshness-gate test.
289... 
290... Report all four as one table — worth more than an extra feature.

395... ## Appendix — Domain reality check: analyst day, ALCO pack, STR filing
396... 
397... *What follows distinguishes verified regulatory/structural facts from reconstructed practitioner texture — an honest accounting of confidence levels.*
398... 
399... ### An AML analyst's day
400... 
401... Queue-driven, not investigation-driven, for most of the day.
402... 
403... - **Morning: the queue.** Case management tool (Actimize, SAS AML, or in-house) opens to alerts generated overnight, ranked by priority tier. Convention: P1 (high risk) triaged within 24 hours, P2 within 5–10 business days, P3 within 30 days.
404... - **Triage dominates volume.** Is this a duplicate, obviously explainable, or does it need real work? A defining industry fact: **80–95% of alerts are false positives** — most of the day is defensibly closing alerts that were never real.
405... - **Real investigations are manual.** Swivel-chair across transaction monitoring, core banking, a separate screening tool, KYC files, and related alerts — manually stitched into a narrative.
406... - **Disposition:** close with documented rationale, escalate, or open a case heading toward a filing. Regulators inspect whether the reasoning and evidence are documented well enough to reconstruct the decision later — not just whether the decision was correct. Thin documentation on a correct decision still draws findings.
407... - Constant deadline pressure from statutory filing clocks running parallel to the triage queue, plus quality-review sampling.
408... 
409... ### An STR filing (India / FIU-IND)
410... 
411... - **Trigger:** a transaction or pattern that's unusual, lacks economic rationale, or is inconsistent with the customer's known profile — the Principal Officer forms a "suspicion."
412... - **Clock:** filed within **7 working days** of forming that suspicion (vs. CTR, a monthly aggregate for cash activity over ₹10 lakh, due by the 15th of the next month).
413... - **Who signs it:** every reporting entity designates a **Principal Officer** under Rule 7 of the PML Rules, who bears filing responsibility — not the analyst who found it. This is why the design uses maker-checker, not auto-submission.
414... - **Format:** filed electronically through FINGate 2.0 as structured XML conforming to FIU-IND's reporting format guide (Transaction Based or Account Based Reporting Format) — not free text. The filing is a narrative plus a structured schema that must validate before acceptance.
415... - **Narrative contents:** factual chronology (dates, amounts, counterparties, channels), the specific inconsistency with stated occupation/business/income, prior alerts on the same customer, and reasoning written to stand alone — FIU-IND analysts read it with zero other context.
416... 
417... ### An ALCO pack
418... 
419... ALCO (Asset-Liability Committee) is headed by the CEO/CMD or an ED, with the Board's management committee overseeing it. The pack is a set of standardised statements, not a discretionary report:
420... 
421... - **Statement of Structural Liquidity** — the maturity-bucketed gap statement. Original RBI guidelines: negative gap not exceeding **20%** of cash outflows in 1–14 day and 15–28 day buckets; later refined to finer buckets: **5%, 10%, 15%, 20%** for Next-day/2–7/8–14/15–28 day buckets (bank ALM framework). The NBFC-specific 2019 framework uses **10%/10%/20%** for 1–7/8–14/15–30 days — a related but distinct number set; use the NBFC numbers for this build.
422... - **Statement of Short-Term Dynamic Liquidity** — rolling forward-looking cash flow across a 1–90 day horizon, prepared more frequently than regulatory submission requires.
423... - **Statement of Interest Rate Sensitivity** — repricing gap between rate-sensitive assets and liabilities, determining asset-sensitivity vs. liability-sensitivity to rate moves.
424... - Alongside these: deposit concentration, investment/treasury book exposure, often a liquidity stress test/contingency funding plan view, and board-fixed tolerances per bucket — any breach requires documented explanation and, in some frameworks, Board approval to operate above the limit.
425... 
426... The pack goes to ALCO first, then to the **Board** — a governance artifact with its own paper trail, structurally parallel to the STR.
427... 
428... ### Honest confidence note
429... 
430... The **regulatory skeleton** — filing deadlines, bucket structures, threshold percentages, who signs what — is grounded in primary sources (RBI circulars, PML Rules, FIU-IND documentation) and can be cited precisely. The **lived texture** — what it feels like to work a 1,400-alert Monday queue, the specific friction points a supervisor pushes back on — is reconstructed from how vendors, consultants, and regulators describe the job, not from direct practitioner experience. Before building the demo script around the "Priya" persona, it's worth pressure-testing that narrative against a real practitioner account (ACAMS forum threads, Wolfsberg Group publications, or AML analyst interviews) so the demo doesn't unintentionally recite vendor marketing copy as lived experience.

Risk & Compliance Copilot

Developer Quickstart — from zero to demo

The one-sentence pitch: An AML analyst's copilot that goes from suspicious signal all the way to a regulator-ready STR filing — where every number comes from SQL, never from an LLM.

1. The Big Picture (30 seconds)

The whole system is a pipeline with 4 stages. Everything else is plumbing to make these stages work.

flowchart LR
    S["SIGNAL\nRule fires on data"]
    E["EVIDENCE\nImmutable pointers\nto source rows"]
    F["FINDING\nLLM-composed\nnarrative + citations"]
    A["ARTIFACT\nSTR filing XML\nready for sign-off"]
    S --> E --> F --> A
1
Signal
Deterministic SQL rules fire on transaction patterns (structuring, income mismatch, sanctions match). No ML. No LLM.
2
Evidence
Pointers (not copies) to the actual rows — txn IDs, party records, policy clauses. Each carries a Snowflake query_id for reproducibility.
3
Finding
An LLM composes a narrative citing the evidence. Versioned, never updated. Every claim must resolve to an evidence row.
4
Artifact
The FIU-IND STR XML file. All numbers from SQL. A human Principal Officer must sign off — auto-filing is legally wrong.
The Golden Rule

No number in a regulatory filing is ever produced by a language model. Every figure comes from a SQL query. The LLM only selects, sequences, and narrates.

2. What You're Actually Building

Data Flow (simplified)

Raw data enters on the left, signals come out on the right. There are two speeds: fast (fraud/AML, minutes) and slow (credit risk, daily).

flowchart LR
    subgraph RAW["Raw Landing"]
        R1["RAW_TRANSACTIONS"]
        R2["RAW_PARTY_CBS\nRAW_PARTY_KYC"]
        R3["RAW_SANCTIONS"]
    end
    subgraph DT["Dynamic Tables"]
        D1["DT_DIM_PARTY\n1 day"]
        D2["DT_ENRICHED\n1 min"]
        D3["DT_VELOCITY\ndownstream"]
        D4["DT_SANCTIONS\ndownstream"]
        D5["DT_SIGNALS_FAST\n5 min"]
    end
    subgraph OUT["Outputs"]
        SIG["SIGNAL rows"]
        CASE["CASE created"]
    end
    R1 --> D2
    R2 --> D1 --> D2
    D2 --> D3 --> D5
    R3 --> D4 --> D5
    D5 -->|"stream + task"| SIG --> CASE

The 4 Agents

Four Cortex Agents with distinct roles. They hand off cases to each other:

flowchart LR
    SE["SENTINEL\nTriage + prioritize\nnew cases"]
    IN["INVESTIGATOR\nGather evidence\nusing tools"]
    DR["DRAFTER\nCompose finding\n+ STR XML"]
    RE["REVIEWER\nAdversarial check\nevery claim"]
    SE --> IN --> DR --> RE
    RE -->|"REJECT"| DR
    RE -->|"APPROVE"| HU["Human\nPrincipal Officer\nsigns off"]
Sentinel
Reads new signals, opens cases, sets priority. Mostly deterministic — LLM only for ranking summary.
Investigator
Heavy tool use: queries semantic view, searches sanctions, traverses counterparty graph. Writes EVIDENCE rows. No conclusions.
Drafter
Reads evidence bundle, maps to policy clauses, writes FINDING narrative + STR XML. Every number from SQL.
Reviewer (Critic)
Recomputes every numeric claim, checks citations resolve, verifies clauses in effect. APPROVE or REJECT with specific defects.

3. Where the Data Comes From

Three layers, three technologies. This is important — don't use an LLM to generate transactions.

LayerWhatHowOutput
L1 — Entities Parties, accounts, relationships Python Faker (hi_IN locale) + custom graph builder. Seeded for reproducibility. ~5K parties, ~10K accounts, UBO graph edges
L2 — Transactions The behavioral ledger IBM AMLworld HI-Small dataset, re-skinned to INR/India. Labels are deterministic ground truth. ~5M txns with known laundering patterns
L3 — Narratives KYC notes, case comments, policies AI_COMPLETE via Cortex. Bulk = small model. Golden docs = frontier model. 10K KYC notes, internal AML policy docs
L2 Re-skin Is Non-Trivial

IBM AMLworld is pair-level (sender to receiver). Your schema is leg-level (one row per debit, one per credit). Each AMLworld row becomes two rows. The reskin_transactions.py script must handle: currency conversion (x83 for INR), channel remapping (ACH to NEFT, Wire to RTGS), and this pair-to-leg split.

4. Build Order (17 Steps)

This is the critical path. Each step depends on the ones before it. Don't skip ahead.

1
Core DDL — 16 tables across 6 schemas sql/01_ddl.sql

Create all tables from the ER model. Schemas: RAW, CURATED, GOVERNANCE, EVIDENCE_CHAIN, AUDIT, GROUND_TRUTH.

2
L1 Entity Generator scripts/generate_entities.py

Faker with hi_IN locale. ~5K parties with Indian names, PAN/Aadhaar-style IDs, graph edges for relationships.

3
L2 Transaction Reskin scripts/reskin_transactions.py

Read HI-Small, convert to INR, remap channels, split pairs to legs, separate labels to GROUND_TRUTH.LABELS.

4
L3 Narrative Generator scripts/generate_narratives.sql

AI_COMPLETE calls to generate KYC notes and case comments. Inject correlated noise (typos, contradictions with structured records).

5
Replay Harness scripts/replay_harness.py

Python script: reads transactions in timestamp order, INSERTs batches, sleeps. --inject structuring_burst flag for live demo.

6
6 Dynamic Tables sql/02_dynamic_tables.sql

DT_DIM_PARTY (1d), DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED (1m), DT_TXN_VELOCITY_FEATURES (downstream), DT_SANCTIONS_CONSOLIDATED (downstream), DT_PARTY_RELATIONSHIP (1d), DT_SIGNALS_FAST (5m).

7
Stream + Routing Task sql/03_stream_task.sql

SIGNALS_STREAM on DT_SIGNALS_FAST. ROUTE_SIGNALS task creates CASE + SIGNAL rows when stream has data.

8
Policy Clause Population sql/05_policy_ingest.sql

AI_PARSE_DOCUMENT + AI_EXTRACT on 8 real regulatory PDFs. Extract clause-level structured data.

9
Cortex Search Service sql/06_search_service.sql

Hybrid keyword + semantic search over policy clause chunks. Carries (doc, section, clause, effective_date) metadata.

10
Semantic View + 20 Verified Queries semantic_views/risk_copilot.yaml

Physical tables: all 6 DTs + POLICY_CLAUSE + CASE + SIGNAL + EVIDENCE + FINDING. 20 pre-authored verified queries.

11
4 Cortex Agents sql/04_agents.sql

Sentinel, Investigator, Drafter, Reviewer. Build Reviewer FIRST — it's the highest demo-ROI agent.

12
7 Stored Procedures (Agent Tools) sql/procedures/*.sql

open_case, gather_evidence_bundle, screen_sanctions_batch, traverse_counterparty_graph, generate_str_xml, validate_filing_schema, escalate_to_principal_officer.

13
RLS + Masking Policies sql/07_governance.sql

Row-level security on PARTY + TRANSACTION (branch-level). Masking on PAN/Aadhaar. Demo: same question, two roles, different answers.

14
Evaluation Suite 1 — Detection F1 tests/test_detection.sql

Per-typology Precision/Recall/F1 against GROUND_TRUTH.LABELS. Target: F1 > 0.7 for structuring.

15
Evaluation Suite 2 — Text-to-SQL tests/golden_questions.sql

15-20 golden questions with expected results. Measured on result match, not SQL match. Target: >85%.

16
3 Scheduled Automations automations/

Overnight triage (daily 02:00), monthly CTR pre-assembly (1st), weekly regulatory-change check (Sun 22:00).

17
Streamlit App app/streamlit_app.py

Dashboard + investigation interface. Build LAST. This is the presentation layer, not the core.

5. The Tables That Matter Most

16 tables is a lot. Here are the 7 you'll touch constantly:

TableSchemaWhat It HoldsKey Columns
RAW_TRANSACTIONSRAWEvery transaction leg (append-only)txn_id, account_id, amount (signed), channel, txn_timestamp
PARTYCURATEDCustomer/counterparty profilesparty_id, risk_rating, pep_flag, declared_annual_income

CASEEVIDENCE_CHAINInvestigation cases (grouped signals)case_id, party_id, case_type, status, sla_deadline
EVIDENCEEVIDENCE_CHAINPointers to source dataevidence_id, case_id, ref_type, ref_id, query_id, as_of_ts

POLICY_CLAUSEGOVERNANCEStructured regulatory rulesclause_id, metric, operator, threshold_lower, effective_from

6. The 3 Detection Rules You Must Build

These go into DT_SIGNALS_FAST. Each one is a SQL query that produces SIGNAL-shaped rows.

STRUCTURING_CROSS_ACCOUNT
Sub-threshold cash deposits split across multiple accounts of the same party, totaling near or above the Rs 10L CTR trigger. Look for amounts between Rs 9.4L-9.8L per account per month.
INCOME_ACTIVITY_MISMATCH
30-day inflows exceed N times the party's declared annual income (from KYC). A salaried employee declaring Rs 8L/year receiving Rs 50L in a month.
SANCTIONS_MATCH_NEW
A party matches a sanctions entry added since the last check. Join DT_DIM_PARTY against DT_SANCTIONS_CONSOLIDATED on name similarity.

7. The 6-Minute Demo

Anchored to "Priya," an AML analyst at a mid-size NBFC. Monday morning, STR clock ticking.

gantt
    title Demo Script (6 minutes)
    dateFormat X

The Money Shot (3:15-4:00)

Draft an STR with a planted defect (e.g., wrong threshold citation). The Reviewer agent catches it, rejects with a specific reason. Regenerate. Passes. This is the single most memorable demo moment.

8. Issues and Inconsistencies Found

These are problems in the design doc that will bite you during implementation. Address them before or during coding.

ISSUE 1: Table Count Mismatch

Section 26 says "16 tables across 6 schemas." Section 29 (DDL spec) says to create 16 tables from Diagram 1 plus 3 staging tables (RAW_TRANSACTIONS, RAW_ACCOUNTS, RAW_SANCTIONS_OPENSANCTIONS) plus GROUND_TRUTH.LABELS — that's 20. Meanwhile, the ER diagram (Diagram 1) shows 16 entities but some of these (like PARTY_RELATIONSHIP) overlap with the DT definitions (DT_PARTY_RELATIONSHIP). Are the DTs replacing the base tables, or do both exist? The doc never clarifies which of the 16 ER entities become regular tables and which become DTs.

ISSUE 2: DT_DIM_PARTY — SCD2 Contradiction

Diagram 15 (Storage Model) labels DT_DIM_PARTY as "1 day, SCD2". But the Fatal Gaps section (Gap 2) explicitly says "MOVED TO FUTURE SCOPE — for the hackathon, DT_DIM_PARTY is current-state only (no effective_from/effective_to)." And Section 26 (Future Scope) confirms SCD2 is deferred. The ER diagram for PARTY still shows effective_from/effective_to columns. You'll need to decide: either remove those SCD2 columns from the DDL, or keep them but leave them NULL. The design doc contradicts itself.

ISSUE 3: RAPID_CREDIT_VELOCITY — Ghost Signal

The Demo Spine (Diagram 14) describes a key demo signal called "RAPID_CREDIT_VELOCITY" (12 credits, 8 remitters, Rs 47L in 3 days). But this signal does not appear anywhere in the Tier 1 signals list (Diagram 5). The Tier 1 signals are STRUCTURING_CROSS_ACCOUNT, INCOME_ACTIVITY_MISMATCH, and SANCTIONS_MATCH_NEW. Either the demo spine relies on a signal you haven't built, or you need to add RAPID_CREDIT_VELOCITY as a 4th rule in DT_SIGNALS_FAST.

ISSUE 4: SHARED_DEVICE_CLUSTER — No Device Data

The Demo Spine also relies on "SHARED_DEVICE_CLUSTER" (3 accounts share a device fingerprint). But the IBM AMLworld dataset has no device data — it's a pure transaction ledger. The L1 entity generator spec doesn't mention generating device fingerprints either. The PARTY_RELATIONSHIP table has SHARED_DEVICE as an edge type, but there's no specified data source for it. You'll need to explicitly generate device fingerprints in L1 and inject shared-device patterns.

ISSUE 5: MULE_RING_CANDIDATE in Demo — It's Tier 2

The demo spine shows MULE_RING_CANDIDATE as the third signal for the demo entity. But Diagram 5 explicitly marks it as an "ON-DEMAND AGENT TOOL (not a DT)" because recursive CTEs can't be incrementally refreshed. And Section 26 puts it in Tier 2. The demo script assumes it exists, but the build plan says build it only "if time." Either adjust the demo spine or move this to Tier 1.

WARNING 1: Velocity Features — DT Feasibility

DT_TXN_VELOCITY_FEATURES needs rolling 1h/24h/7d/30d windows. Dynamic tables do incremental refresh, but true sliding windows (e.g., "count of transactions in the last 24 hours") require recomputing against the time boundary on every refresh — not just on newly arrived rows. At scale, this may force full refreshes. The doc doesn't address this. You may need tumbling windows (fixed daily buckets) instead of true sliding windows.

WARNING 2: 4 Agents = 4 Separate Cortex Agents?

The design describes 4 agent "roles" with explicit handoffs (Sentinel passes to Investigator, etc.). But Cortex Agents don't have a native multi-agent orchestration framework — each agent is independent. The handoff logic (Sentinel triggers Investigator, etc.) would need to be implemented via tasks, streams, or stored procedures calling agents. The doc doesn't specify how agent-to-agent handoffs actually work in Snowflake. Consider: a single agent with 4 modes (via system prompt switching) may be simpler for a hackathon than 4 independent agents with custom orchestration.

WARNING 3: RESULT_SCAN(query_id) for Reproducibility

The Evidence Pointer Resolution (Gap 5) says the Reviewer can re-execute queries using RESULT_SCAN(query_id). But RESULT_SCAN only works for queries within the same session and results persist for only 24 hours. For cross-session reproducibility, you'd need to re-run the original SQL with AT(TIMESTAMP => as_of_ts) — which requires Time Travel retention to still be active. The 24-hour RESULT_SCAN window makes the proposed approach fragile for any case older than a day.

WARNING 4: Sanctions — Dual Approach Complexity

Gap 3 decides to use BOTH an exact join in DT_SIGNALS_FAST AND a daily CORTEX_SEARCH_BATCH. But the DT approach (exact/near-exact join against DT_SANCTIONS_CONSOLIDATED) is what fires the SANCTIONS_MATCH_NEW signal in near-real-time. The daily batch (fuzzy matching the full party book) writes to a SCREENING_RESULT table — but this table doesn't appear in the ER model, storage model, or semantic view spec. It's a phantom table that feeds into an unspecified workflow.

WARNING 5: "20 Verified Queries" — Only Titles Listed

The doc references "20 verified queries from Section 23" but the actual architecture doc only lists query titles and brief descriptions. The actual SQL for these verified queries hasn't been written. This is a significant chunk of work that's easy to underestimate — each verified query needs to be authored, tested against real data, and validated for correctness.

content.displayText: Explain what these "Python Faker (hi_IN locale) + custom graph builder. Seeded for reproducibility." in L1 mean

content.text:
**Faker** is a Python library that generates realistic fake data. When you do:

```python
from faker import Faker
fake = Faker('hi_IN')  # hi_IN = Hindi/India locale

fake.name()              # → "Aarav Sharma"
fake.address()           # → "42, MG Road, Pune, Maharashtra 411001"
fake.phone_number()      # → "+91 98765 43210"
```

The `hi_IN` locale makes it generate Indian names, addresses, phone formats, etc. instead of US/European defaults.

**"Seeded for reproducibility"** means you set a fixed random seed:

```python
Faker.seed(42)
```

Now every run produces the exact same "random" data. If a judge or teammate runs your script, they get identical parties, accounts, and relationships. Without a seed, you'd get different names and IDs every time, which breaks referential integrity with the transaction data.

**"Custom graph builder"** means Faker alone only generates flat records (one party at a time). It doesn't know that Party A owns Account X, or that Party B is the beneficial owner of Party C. You need custom Python code on top of Faker to:

- Create ownership edges (party owns account)
- Create UBO chains (Party A owns 60% of Company B which owns Account C)
- Create shared-attribute edges (two parties share a phone number or device)
- Create director/guarantor links

This is the "graph" — the relationship network between entities. Something like:

```python
# Pseudocode — not from the repo, just illustrating the concept
for party in parties:
    accounts = assign_accounts(party, count=random.randint(1, 4))
    for acc in accounts:
        relationships.append(("OWNS_ACCOUNT", party.id, acc.id))
    
    # 5% of parties share a phone with another party
    if random.random() < 0.05:
        other = random.choice(parties)
        relationships.append(("SHARED_PHONE", party.id, other.id))
```

This outputs the `PARTY`, `ACCOUNT`, and `PARTY_RELATIONSHIP` tables (the ~5K parties, ~10K accounts, and graph edges referenced in the build plan). The transaction layer (L2) then operates on top of these entities.
Can we set that the percentage in related accounts as well with Faker?
content.displayText: Can we set that the percentage in related accounts as well with Faker?

content.text:
No. Faker doesn't do relationships at all. It generates one record at a time with no concept of "this party connects to that account." The percentages and graph structure are entirely your custom code.

Faker's job ends at producing realistic-looking field values — names, addresses, PAN numbers. Everything about *how entities relate to each other* (ownership rates, shared-attribute probabilities, UBO chain depths) is logic you write yourself.

So a typical split would be:

```python
# Faker's job: realistic field values

Let me explain the device fingerprint question.

When you use a banking app, the bank records the device you're using — a hash like `d8f3a2b1...` derived from your phone's hardware/browser properties. That's a **device fingerprint**.

In real fraud, mule accounts operated by the same person often share the same phone. "3 accounts, same device fingerprint, with fund flows between them" is the SHARED_DEVICE_CLUSTER signal.

IBM AMLworld doesn't have this data — it's just transactions. So you need to **generate** it synthetically in your L1 entity script. The question is where to store it:

options.description: Add a device_fingerprint VARCHAR column directly to the ACCOUNT table. During L1 generation, most accounts get a unique fingerprint. ~8% of accounts share a fingerprint with 1-2 others (simulating shared devices). Simple: one column, no extra tables. The SHARED_DEVICE_CLUSTER rule just does GROUP BY device_fingerprint HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3.
options.label: Column on ACCOUNT

L1 generator logic:

Detection query:

  FROM DT_DIM_ACCOUNT
  GROUP BY device_fingerprint
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3

  HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT account_id) >= 3

Risk & Compliance Copilot

Developer Quickstart — from zero to demo

The one-sentence pitch: An AML analyst's copilot that goes from suspicious signal all the way to a regulator-ready STR filing — where every number comes from SQL, never from an LLM.

1. The Big Picture (30 seconds)

The whole system is a pipeline with 4 stages. Everything else is plumbing to make these stages work.

flowchart LR
    S["SIGNAL\nRule fires on data"]
    E["EVIDENCE\nImmutable pointers\nto source rows"]
    F["FINDING\nLLM-composed\nnarrative + citations"]
    A["ARTIFACT\nSTR filing XML\nready for sign-off"]
    S --> E --> F --> A
1
Signal
Deterministic SQL rules fire on transaction patterns (structuring, income mismatch, sanctions match). No ML. No LLM.
2
Evidence
Pointers (not copies) to the actual rows — txn IDs, party records, policy clauses. Each carries a Snowflake query_id for reproducibility.
3
Finding
An LLM composes a narrative citing the evidence. Versioned, never updated. Every claim must resolve to an evidence row.
4
Artifact
The FIU-IND STR XML file. All numbers from SQL. A human Principal Officer must sign off — auto-filing is legally wrong.
The Golden Rule

No number in a regulatory filing is ever produced by a language model. Every figure comes from a SQL query. The LLM only selects, sequences, and narrates.

2. What You're Actually Building

Data Flow (simplified)

Raw data enters on the left, signals come out on the right. There are two speeds: fast (fraud/AML, minutes) and slow (credit risk, daily).

    subgraph RAW["Raw Landing"]
        R1["RAW_TRANSACTIONS"]
        R2["RAW_PARTY_CBS\nRAW_PARTY_KYC"]
        R3["RAW_SANCTIONS"]
    end
    subgraph DT["Dynamic Tables"]
        D1["DT_DIM_PARTY\n1 day"]
        D2["DT_ENRICHED\n1 min"]
        D3["DT_VELOCITY\ndownstream"]
        D4["DT_SANCTIONS\ndownstream"]
        D5["DT_SIGNALS_FAST\n5 min"]
    end
    subgraph OUT["Outputs"]
        SIG["SIGNAL rows"]
        CASE["CASE created"]
    end
    R1 --> D2
    R2 --> D1 --> D2
    D2 --> D3 --> D5
    R3 --> D4 --> D5
    D5 -->|"stream + task"| SIG --> CASE

The 4 Agents

Four Cortex Agents with distinct roles. They hand off cases to each other:

flowchart LR
    SE["SENTINEL\nTriage + prioritize\nnew cases"]
    IN["INVESTIGATOR\nGather evidence\nusing tools"]
    DR["DRAFTER\nCompose finding\n+ STR XML"]
    RE["REVIEWER\nAdversarial check\nevery claim"]
    SE --> IN --> DR --> RE
    RE -->|"REJECT"| DR
    RE -->|"APPROVE"| HU["Human\nPrincipal Officer\nsigns off"]
Sentinel
Reads new signals, opens cases, sets priority. Mostly deterministic — LLM only for ranking summary.
Investigator
Heavy tool use: queries semantic view, searches sanctions, traverses counterparty graph. Writes EVIDENCE rows. No conclusions.
Drafter
Reads evidence bundle, maps to policy clauses, writes FINDING narrative + STR XML. Every number from SQL.
Reviewer (Critic)
Recomputes every numeric claim, checks citations resolve, verifies clauses in effect. APPROVE or REJECT with specific defects.

3. Where the Data Comes From

Three layers, three technologies. This is important — don't use an LLM to generate transactions.

LayerWhatHowOutput
L1 — Entities Parties, accounts, relationships Python Faker (hi_IN locale) + custom graph builder. Seeded for reproducibility. ~5K parties, ~10K accounts, UBO graph edges
L2 — Transactions The behavioral ledger IBM AMLworld HI-Small dataset, re-skinned to INR/India. Labels are deterministic ground truth. ~5M txns with known laundering patterns
L3 — Narratives KYC notes, case comments, policies AI_COMPLETE via Cortex. Bulk = small model. Golden docs = frontier model. 10K KYC notes, internal AML policy docs
L2 Re-skin Is Non-Trivial

IBM AMLworld is pair-level (sender to receiver). Your schema is leg-level (one row per debit, one per credit). Each AMLworld row becomes two rows. The reskin_transactions.py script must handle: currency conversion (x83 for INR), channel remapping (ACH to NEFT, Wire to RTGS), and this pair-to-leg split.

6. The 3 Detection Rules You Must Build

These go into DT_SIGNALS_FAST. Each one is a SQL query that produces SIGNAL-shaped rows.

STRUCTURING_CROSS_ACCOUNT
Sub-threshold cash deposits split across multiple accounts of the same party, totaling near or above the Rs 10L CTR trigger. Look for amounts between Rs 9.4L-9.8L per account per month.
INCOME_ACTIVITY_MISMATCH
30-day inflows exceed N times the party's declared annual income (from KYC). A salaried employee declaring Rs 8L/year receiving Rs 50L in a month.
SANCTIONS_MATCH_NEW
A party matches a sanctions entry added since the last check. Join DT_DIM_PARTY against DT_SANCTIONS_CONSOLIDATED on name similarity.

Draft an STR with a planted defect (e.g., wrong threshold citation). The Reviewer agent catches it, rejects with a specific reason. Regenerate. Passes. This is the single most memorable demo moment.

8. Issues and Inconsistencies Found

These are problems in the design doc that will bite you during implementation. Address them before or during coding.

ISSUE 1: Table Count Mismatch

Section 26 says "16 tables across 6 schemas." Section 29 (DDL spec) says to create 16 tables from Diagram 1 plus 3 staging tables (RAW_TRANSACTIONS, RAW_ACCOUNTS, RAW_SANCTIONS_OPENSANCTIONS) plus GROUND_TRUTH.LABELS — that's 20. Meanwhile, the ER diagram (Diagram 1) shows 16 entities but some of these (like PARTY_RELATIONSHIP) overlap with the DT definitions (DT_PARTY_RELATIONSHIP). Are the DTs replacing the base tables, or do both exist? The doc never clarifies which of the 16 ER entities become regular tables and which become DTs.

ISSUE 2: DT_DIM_PARTY — SCD2 Contradiction

Diagram 15 (Storage Model) labels DT_DIM_PARTY as "1 day, SCD2". But the Fatal Gaps section (Gap 2) explicitly says "MOVED TO FUTURE SCOPE — for the hackathon, DT_DIM_PARTY is current-state only (no effective_from/effective_to)." And Section 26 (Future Scope) confirms SCD2 is deferred. The ER diagram for PARTY still shows effective_from/effective_to columns. You'll need to decide: either remove those SCD2 columns from the DDL, or keep them but leave them NULL. The design doc contradicts itself.

ISSUE 3: RAPID_CREDIT_VELOCITY — Ghost Signal

The Demo Spine (Diagram 14) describes a key demo signal called "RAPID_CREDIT_VELOCITY" (12 credits, 8 remitters, Rs 47L in 3 days). But this signal does not appear anywhere in the Tier 1 signals list (Diagram 5). The Tier 1 signals are STRUCTURING_CROSS_ACCOUNT, INCOME_ACTIVITY_MISMATCH, and SANCTIONS_MATCH_NEW. Either the demo spine relies on a signal you haven't built, or you need to add RAPID_CREDIT_VELOCITY as a 4th rule in DT_SIGNALS_FAST.

ISSUE 4: SHARED_DEVICE_CLUSTER — No Device Data

The Demo Spine also relies on "SHARED_DEVICE_CLUSTER" (3 accounts share a device fingerprint). But the IBM AMLworld dataset has no device data — it's a pure transaction ledger. The L1 entity generator spec doesn't mention generating device fingerprints either. The PARTY_RELATIONSHIP table has SHARED_DEVICE as an edge type, but there's no specified data source for it. You'll need to explicitly generate device fingerprints in L1 and inject shared-device patterns.

ISSUE 5: MULE_RING_CANDIDATE in Demo — It's Tier 2

The demo spine shows MULE_RING_CANDIDATE as the third signal for the demo entity. But Diagram 5 explicitly marks it as an "ON-DEMAND AGENT TOOL (not a DT)" because recursive CTEs can't be incrementally refreshed. And Section 26 puts it in Tier 2. The demo script assumes it exists, but the build plan says build it only "if time." Either adjust the demo spine or move this to Tier 1.

WARNING 1: Velocity Features — DT Feasibility

DT_TXN_VELOCITY_FEATURES needs rolling 1h/24h/7d/30d windows. Dynamic tables do incremental refresh, but true sliding windows (e.g., "count of transactions in the last 24 hours") require recomputing against the time boundary on every refresh — not just on newly arrived rows. At scale, this may force full refreshes. The doc doesn't address this. You may need tumbling windows (fixed daily buckets) instead of true sliding windows.

WARNING 2: 4 Agents = 4 Separate Cortex Agents?

The design describes 4 agent "roles" with explicit handoffs (Sentinel passes to Investigator, etc.). But Cortex Agents don't have a native multi-agent orchestration framework — each agent is independent. The handoff logic (Sentinel triggers Investigator, etc.) would need to be implemented via tasks, streams, or stored procedures calling agents. The doc doesn't specify how agent-to-agent handoffs actually work in Snowflake. Consider: a single agent with 4 modes (via system prompt switching) may be simpler for a hackathon than 4 independent agents with custom orchestration.

WARNING 3: RESULT_SCAN(query_id) for Reproducibility

The Evidence Pointer Resolution (Gap 5) says the Reviewer can re-execute queries using RESULT_SCAN(query_id). But RESULT_SCAN only works for queries within the same session and results persist for only 24 hours. For cross-session reproducibility, you'd need to re-run the original SQL with AT(TIMESTAMP => as_of_ts) — which requires Time Travel retention to still be active. The 24-hour RESULT_SCAN window makes the proposed approach fragile for any case older than a day.

WARNING 4: Sanctions — Dual Approach Complexity

Gap 3 decides to use BOTH an exact join in DT_SIGNALS_FAST AND a daily CORTEX_SEARCH_BATCH. But the DT approach (exact/near-exact join against DT_SANCTIONS_CONSOLIDATED) is what fires the SANCTIONS_MATCH_NEW signal in near-real-time. The daily batch (fuzzy matching the full party book) writes to a SCREENING_RESULT table — but this table doesn't appear in the ER model, storage model, or semantic view spec. It's a phantom table that feeds into an unspecified workflow.

WARNING 5: "20 Verified Queries" — Only Titles Listed

The doc references "20 verified queries from Section 23" but the actual architecture doc only lists query titles and brief descriptions. The actual SQL for these verified queries hasn't been written. This is a significant chunk of work that's easy to underestimate — each verified query needs to be authored, tested against real data, and validated for correctness.

6. The 5 Detection Rules + 1 Agent Tool

8. Issues and Inconsistencies Found

These are problems in the design doc that will bite you during implementation. Address them before or during coding.

ISSUE 1: Table Count Mismatch

Section 26 says "16 tables across 6 schemas." Section 29 (DDL spec) says to create 16 tables from Diagram 1 plus 3 staging tables (RAW_TRANSACTIONS, RAW_ACCOUNTS, RAW_SANCTIONS_OPENSANCTIONS) plus GROUND_TRUTH.LABELS — that's 20. Meanwhile, the ER diagram (Diagram 1) shows 16 entities but some of these (like PARTY_RELATIONSHIP) overlap with the DT definitions (DT_PARTY_RELATIONSHIP). Are the DTs replacing the base tables, or do both exist? The doc never clarifies which of the 16 ER entities become regular tables and which become DTs.

ISSUE 2: DT_DIM_PARTY — SCD2 Contradiction

Diagram 15 (Storage Model) labels DT_DIM_PARTY as "1 day, SCD2". But the Fatal Gaps section (Gap 2) explicitly says "MOVED TO FUTURE SCOPE — for the hackathon, DT_DIM_PARTY is current-state only (no effective_from/effective_to)." And Section 26 (Future Scope) confirms SCD2 is deferred. The ER diagram for PARTY still shows effective_from/effective_to columns. You'll need to decide: either remove those SCD2 columns from the DDL, or keep them but leave them NULL. The design doc contradicts itself.

ISSUE 3: RAPID_CREDIT_VELOCITY — Ghost Signal

The Demo Spine (Diagram 14) describes a key demo signal called "RAPID_CREDIT_VELOCITY" (12 credits, 8 remitters, Rs 47L in 3 days). But this signal does not appear anywhere in the Tier 1 signals list (Diagram 5). The Tier 1 signals are STRUCTURING_CROSS_ACCOUNT, INCOME_ACTIVITY_MISMATCH, and SANCTIONS_MATCH_NEW. Either the demo spine relies on a signal you haven't built, or you need to add RAPID_CREDIT_VELOCITY as a 4th rule in DT_SIGNALS_FAST.

ISSUE 4: SHARED_DEVICE_CLUSTER — No Device Data

The Demo Spine also relies on "SHARED_DEVICE_CLUSTER" (3 accounts share a device fingerprint). But the IBM AMLworld dataset has no device data — it's a pure transaction ledger. The L1 entity generator spec doesn't mention generating device fingerprints either. The PARTY_RELATIONSHIP table has SHARED_DEVICE as an edge type, but there's no specified data source for it. You'll need to explicitly generate device fingerprints in L1 and inject shared-device patterns.

ISSUE 5: MULE_RING_CANDIDATE in Demo — It's Tier 2

The demo spine shows MULE_RING_CANDIDATE as the third signal for the demo entity. But Diagram 5 explicitly marks it as an "ON-DEMAND AGENT TOOL (not a DT)" because recursive CTEs can't be incrementally refreshed. And Section 26 puts it in Tier 2. The demo script assumes it exists, but the build plan says build it only "if time." Either adjust the demo spine or move this to Tier 1.

WARNING 1: Velocity Features — DT Feasibility

DT_TXN_VELOCITY_FEATURES needs rolling 1h/24h/7d/30d windows. Dynamic tables do incremental refresh, but true sliding windows (e.g., "count of transactions in the last 24 hours") require recomputing against the time boundary on every refresh — not just on newly arrived rows. At scale, this may force full refreshes. The doc doesn't address this. You may need tumbling windows (fixed daily buckets) instead of true sliding windows.

WARNING 2: 4 Agents = 4 Separate Cortex Agents?

The design describes 4 agent "roles" with explicit handoffs (Sentinel passes to Investigator, etc.). But Cortex Agents don't have a native multi-agent orchestration framework — each agent is independent. The handoff logic (Sentinel triggers Investigator, etc.) would need to be implemented via tasks, streams, or stored procedures calling agents. The doc doesn't specify how agent-to-agent handoffs actually work in Snowflake. Consider: a single agent with 4 modes (via system prompt switching) may be simpler for a hackathon than 4 independent agents with custom orchestration.

WARNING 3: RESULT_SCAN(query_id) for Reproducibility

The Evidence Pointer Resolution (Gap 5) says the Reviewer can re-execute queries using RESULT_SCAN(query_id). But RESULT_SCAN only works for queries within the same session and results persist for only 24 hours. For cross-session reproducibility, you'd need to re-run the original SQL with AT(TIMESTAMP => as_of_ts) — which requires Time Travel retention to still be active. The 24-hour RESULT_SCAN window makes the proposed approach fragile for any case older than a day.

WARNING 4: Sanctions — Dual Approach Complexity

Gap 3 decides to use BOTH an exact join in DT_SIGNALS_FAST AND a daily CORTEX_SEARCH_BATCH. But the DT approach (exact/near-exact join against DT_SANCTIONS_CONSOLIDATED) is what fires the SANCTIONS_MATCH_NEW signal in near-real-time. The daily batch (fuzzy matching the full party book) writes to a SCREENING_RESULT table — but this table doesn't appear in the ER model, storage model, or semantic view spec. It's a phantom table that feeds into an unspecified workflow.

WARNING 5: "20 Verified Queries" — Only Titles Listed

The doc references "20 verified queries from Section 23" but the actual architecture doc only lists query titles and brief descriptions. The actual SQL for these verified queries hasn't been written. This is a significant chunk of work that's easy to underestimate — each verified query needs to be authored, tested against real data, and validated for correctness.

content.displayText: why not have a separate table to log query id pairing up with the sql text and result_hash instead? would make it looker cleaner. What are the 2 remaining wwarning?

content.text:
**On the separate table:** That's a better design. EVIDENCE stays clean (just pointers), and you get a dedicated `EVIDENCE_QUERY_LOG` table that pairs `(query_log_id, evidence_id, sql_text, result_hash, query_id, as_of_ts)`. The EVIDENCE row just references the log via FK. Advantages:

- EVIDENCE stays slim and readable — it's about *what* was gathered, not *how*
- Multiple queries can back a single evidence row (e.g., a party lookup + a txn lookup both supporting one evidence pointer)
- The Reviewer's verification logic queries one table, not scattered across EVIDENCE rows
- You get a clean audit trail of every query ever run, independent of which case it served

I'll make that change.

**The 2 remaining warnings:**

1. **Velocity Features — DT Feasibility.** DT_TXN_VELOCITY_FEATURES needs rolling 1h/24h/7d/30d windows. True sliding windows ("count in the last 24 hours from *right now*") shift their boundary every second, so the DT can't just process new rows — it has to recompute against the moving time edge. This may force full refreshes instead of incremental. Workaround if it hits: use tumbling windows (fixed calendar-day buckets) instead. This is an implementation-time concern, not a design decision you can resolve upfront.

2. **20 Verified Queries Not Written.** The architecture doc lists 20 query titles and categories but zero actual SQL. Each verified query needs to be written against real loaded data, tested for correctness, and embedded in the semantic view YAML. It's easy to underestimate — this is probably a full work session on its own.

Want me to add the `EVIDENCE_QUERY_LOG` table to both docs now?
yes

D

Design Decisions (Gaps 1-9)

Gap 1: Transaction Grain Conversion

Decided: Each AMLworld pair row becomes two leg rows: one debit (negative amount), one credit (positive amount), sharing a txn_pair_id. Pair-level view for graph queries via self-join.

Gap 2: SCD2 on DIM_PARTY

Future scope. DT_DIM_PARTY is current-state only. No effective_from/effective_to. Columns removed from DDL. SCD2 is a "What Production Would Need" slide item.

Gap 3: Sanctions Screening

Decided: Exact join only. DT_SIGNALS_FAST does exact/near-exact name join against DT_SANCTIONS_CONSOLIDATED. CORTEX_SEARCH_BATCH fuzzy screening and SCREENING_RESULT table dropped. Fuzzy matching is future scope.

Gap 4: Case Deduplication

Decided: "Existing" = CASE with status IN (OPEN, INVESTIGATING, DRAFTED) for same party_id. Multiple signals in same refresh attach to same case. Different signal types merge into case_type = 'CROSS_DOMAIN'.

Gap 5: Evidence Pointer Resolution

Decided: Separate query log table. EVIDENCE stays clean (ref_type, ref_id, as_of_ts). EVIDENCE_QUERY_LOG stores sql_text, result_hash, query_id, executed_at — linked via FK. Reviewer re-runs SQL with AT(TIMESTAMP => as_of_ts) and compares hashes. RESULT_SCAN not used.

Gap 6: STR XML Generation

Decided: generate_str_xml() is a Python stored procedure. Reads FINDING + EVIDENCE for structured fields via SQL. Takes narrative from FINDING.narrative as-is. Assembles with xml.etree. Validates against schema. LLM never touches XML.

Gap 7: Verified Query Inventory

Decided: 20 verified queries across 8 categories: transaction lookup (1-3), velocity (4-6), threshold (7-9), network (10-12), sanctions (13-15), cross-silo (16-17), case status (18-19), refusal (20). SQL not yet written.

Gap 8: RLS Roles

Decided: Two roles: BRANCH_ANALYST_MUMBAI (branch_region = MUMBAI only) and COMPLIANCE_OFFICER (sees all). RLS on DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED + DT_DIM_PARTY. Masking on PAN/Aadhaar fields.

Gap 9: Replay Harness

Decided: Simplified. Python script using snowflake-connector-python, INSERT INTO batches, time.sleep(). --inject structuring_burst flag. No Snowpipe Streaming SDK.
